keep: The idea is named up front in plain words: a gas's push changes by a rule of proportion, and the rule only works counted from true zero.

The picture is the brief's: a sealed cylinder under a piston with a heater, one gauge with gauge and absolute readings, locks on the piston and the heat, a pV chart and a p–T chart whose line extends to zero pressure at −273 °C, a pV ÷ T box, and a receiver skin with the cut-in to cut-out band.

Every number is a control, an assumed example figure, a rounded textbook constant (1 bar, 273) or computed from a shown rule: 4 bar absolute and 3 bar gauge at half volume, 293 to 313 K about 7%, 7.8 bar gauge against the 17.5 bar trap, 1,000 L in the band.

Each misconception the brief names is caught by a puzzle with its own wrong pick: gauge in a ratio (screen 3's 2 bar, screen 13's 25%), Celsius in a ratio (screen 5's 4 bar, screen 9's 14 bar, screen 12's 17.5 bar), a fixed relationship whatever is held (screen 7), and the whole receiver counted as usable (screen 11's 4,500 L).

The analogy is from his trade, an offset voltmeter, reproduces the main result (differences survive an offset, ratios do not) and breaks honestly: voltage has no true zero, pressure and temperature do.

Footnotes sit on words their quotes support, one per sentence: [^3] absolute = gauge + atmosphere, [^2] halving doubles, [^1] pressure with absolute temperature at fixed volume, [^4] fewer motor starts. The validator reports no problems.
fix: Causal step skipped: why a gas's pressure follows volume and kelvin at all. Add one 'One way to picture it' line: the push is molecules striking the walls; half the space means each strikes twice as often, and warmer molecules strike harder and more often.
Causal step skipped: why the gauge reading fails in Boyle's law. Say the gas pushes with the whole 2 bar, of which the gauge shows only the part above the atmosphere.
Causal step skipped: pV ÷ T is asserted. Derive it in a sentence: pressure goes up with kelvin and down with volume, so pV ÷ T stays the same when both rules act together.
Causal step skipped: the band's 1,000 L. Show the Boyle step: 500 L at 9 bar absolute would fill 4,500 L at 1 bar, at 7 bar it fills 3,500 L, and the difference is what the band gives.
Misconception not shown failing hard enough: the 17.5 bar trap is stated but not shown to be absurd. Say it more than doubles the pressure for a 30 °C warming, which is nonsense.
Paragraph 3 carries three ideas (temperature, what is held, the combined law with the receiver). Split it: the temperature line in one, what is held and pV ÷ T in the next.
The free piston's result has no number. Give it: 300 K to 400 K grows 3 L to 4 L at the same 2 bar.
False absolute: 'only the air between the two is usable' reads as if air below cut-in were unusable. Say that between starts only the band is drawn on.

False absolute in ignores: 'letting it expand cools it' holds for a quick expansion that pushes a piston, not every expansion. Say 'a quick squeeze warms a gas and a quick expansion against the piston cools it'.
The brief asks for the ratio box to drift in gauge or °C, not only both together. Make it a three-way choice and give the drift in each.
Phone: the three readouts must wrap at 360 px. Say so in whatAmILookingAt.
Tie the receiver to Motors: each start draws the motor's starting current, which is why fewer starts matter.

shape.ruleInWords: yes, but pV ÷ T and the Boyle step to the band are not derived (fixes 3, 4)
shape.workedExampleWithRealNumbers: yes (1 bar gauge halved to 3 bar gauge; 20 to 40 °C about 7%; 7 bar gauge at 20 °C to about 7.8 bar at 50 °C; 500 L band 1,000 L)
shape.misconceptionShownFailing: yes for gauge, Celsius and fixed relationships; the 17.5 bar trap needs its absurdity said (fix 5)
